title: Connecticut's AI Responsibility and Transparency Act takes effect today
subtitle: The first phase of SB 5 covers frontier-developer duties, employment AI disclosures, generative-AI provenance, and a WARN-notice attribution rule — the most expansive state AI law to enter force this year.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Connecticut's Artificial Intelligence Responsibility and Transparency Act — SB 5 — enters its first phase on October 1. The provisions taking effect today cover frontier-developer duties, employment AI disclosures, generative-AI provenance rules, and a federal WARN-notice attribution requirement. Employers issuing mass-layoff notices must now disclose to the Connecticut Department of Labor whether the layoffs are related to the employer's use of AI or another technological change. Employers using AI in hiring or personnel management face new disclosure obligations toward applicants and employees. The second phase, on January 1, 2027, adds AI companion chatbot rules; the third, on October 1, 2027, covers state agency AI inventories and impact assessments. Connecticut becomes the seventh state to enact a comprehensive AI governance statute.

SB 5 is the most expansive AI law enacted in any 2026 state session, and it reaches further than California's or New York's current statutes on the employment side. The frontier-developer duty is the structural piece: any company building or deploying a frontier model with Connecticut users must publish a safety and security framework and report certain safety incidents. That obligation applies regardless of where the developer is based — the trigger is Connecticut users, not Connecticut headquarters. The WARN-notice attribution rule is also novel: it is the first state law to require employers to tell the government, in writing, whether an AI deployment caused a specific round of layoffs. The data this generates will be the first systematic record anywhere of AI-driven workforce displacement.

The staggered schedule mirrors a pattern that has emerged this year across state AI laws: effective dates spread over 12 to 24 months so compliance programs can ramp. The companion-chatbot rules landing in January 2027 are the piece OpenAI, Meta, and Character.AI have been quietly lobbying against, following the suicide-prevention cases referred to state attorneys general in September. The impact assessments landing in October 2027 will likely become the de facto template for the 15 or so state AI bills already pre-filed for 2027 sessions.

For learners: if you build any product that touches Connecticut users and uses AI for hiring, screening, or any other personnel decision, your disclosure obligations started today. That includes résumé-screening tools, interview scorers, scheduling AIs, and performance-management copilots. The practical first step is a simple one: inventory where AI touches your personnel workflow, publish a plain-English disclosure, and keep a dated copy. State AI compliance is where the near-term legal risk lives, not in federal law.
